Elemental Anatomy Of The Excretory System

Sorin M. Dudea

17. 1. Basic renal anatomy

The kidneys are paired organs located symmetrically in the retroperitoneum. The size of the kidneys depends on the patient’s age as well as on their functional state. In adults, the kidneys measure 10-12 cm in length, 5-6 cm in width with a thickness of 3 cm. The kidneys are bean-shaped organs with a vertical longitudinal axis and anteromedially oriented concavity.

Morphologically, the kidneys present two sides (anterior and posterior), two poles (upper and lower) and two margins: lateral - convex - and medial - concave. The renal hilum is located on the latter. It appears as a vertical cleft with two sides: anterior, smaller, and posterior. The hilum is crossed by the elements of the renal pedicle and is continued, inwards, with a virtual cavity located in the center of the kidney, named renal sinus. The sinus contains the collecting system, vessels, nerves as well as adipose connective tissue. In its periphery up to the hilum, the kidney is coated by a fifibrous cap- sule. The sinus is located in the center of the kidney.

Between the capsule and the sinus is the renal parenchyma, composed of the cortex and the medulla. The renal medulla is deeply located next to the sinus. It is discontinuous, being made up of the Malpighi renal pyramids, numbering 7-14 for each kidney. Each pyramid has, in section, a triangular shape, with the base facing the cortex and the tip, also called the renal papilla, facing the renal sinus in which it protrudes. At the pyramids base lie the arcuate arteries, and the minor calyces are inserted on the papilla. The medulla contains the renal collecting tubules. At the level of the renal papilla, the collecting tubes open in the minor calyces. The renal cortex is located superfificially beneath the renal capsule. At the periphery, it is continuous, and towards the center, it becomes discontinuous, under the form of Bertin renal columns that intercalate between the pyramids and touch the sinus. The cortex contains the renal glomeruli and their tributary tubulovascular system (fifigure 126).

The collecting system. The minor calyces insert on the renal papillae as numerous as these and have dimensions of 8/10 mm. The major calyces (calyx stems), 2-3 in number, result from the union of several minor calyces and converge in the renal pelvis. It has a longitudinal diameter of 2-3 cm. and a transverse size of 1-2 cm., being located partially extrarenal where it continues with the ureter. 154 l III. THE EXCRETORY SYSTEM

17.2. The ureter

The ureter is 25-30 cm long in adults and has a 5-10 mm caliber. Due to its vertical descending paravertebral course, the ureter is, anatomically, divided into two parts. The abdominal portion is subdivided into a lumbar segment (up to the wing of the sacrum) - where it describes relations with the genital vessels, colic vessels and nerves

  • and an iliac segment, up to the terminal line,< where it intersects the iliac vessels, forming a curvature. The pelvic segment has a medially concave course, being subdivided into a parietal segment - attached to the lateral wall of the pelvis, a visceral segment (transverse) located between the bladder and rectum in men, respectively at the base of the broad ligament in women - and an intramural segment 15 mm long, located in the thickness of the bladder wall and ending in the ureteral meatus (fifigure 127)

    17.3. Anatomic setting

    In the retroperitoneum, the kidneys are located in the perirenal space, delimited by the perirenal fascia. Inside this space, the kidneys are wrapped in a fat capsule.

    The anatomical environment of the kidneys can be summarized as follows:

  • posterior to the kidneys are the 12th< rib and the lateral arcuate ligament of the diaphragm. At this level, the subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves pass through the pararenal fat. Via the diaphragm, the kidneys establish relations with the lung bases. Also posteriorly located are the quadratus lumborum and psoas muscles;

  • the anterior anatomic reports of the< kidneys differ. The right kidney comes in relation to the right colonic flflexure, the visceral face of the right hepatic lobe, the descending portion of the duodenum, and the small bowel loops. On the left side, anatomic relations are established with the left colonic flflexure, renal facet of the spleen, body of the pancreas, posterior face of the stomach and the loops of the small intestine;

  • laterally on the right lie the visceral< face of the liver and the ascending colon and on the left the renal facet of the spleen and the descending colon;

  • superior to the kidneys and descending slightly on their medial edges are the adrenal glands;
  • inferior is the retroperitoneal adipose tissue, compartmentalized by the perirenal fascia in the perirenal, anterior pararenal and posterior pararenal spaces.

Sorin M. Dudea

18.1. Conventional radiology methods

18.1.1. (Simple, non-enhanced) renal radiography = kidney- ureter - bladder (KUB)

18.1.1.1.Examination technique.

Simple renal radiography (non-contrast-enhanced) aims to assess the projection area of the urinary tract. The image should include the area between the T11 vertebra and the lower edge of the pubic symphysis. The patient is lying on his back; the projection is AP.

On the obtained image, one assesses: a) Patient preparation (the amount of gas

The landmark used to identify the renal areas is the outer edge of the psoas muscle. The renal areas are located superior and external to the upper third of the psoas.

18.1.4. Renal arteriography

Arteriography is performed by retrograde catheterization of the aorta, starting from the femoral artery (Seldinger technique). Injection of the contrast substance into the aorta, cranial to the emergence of the renal arteries, leads to obtaining global renal arteriography. Selective renal arteriography involves the insertion of the catheter into the trunk of a major renal artery, while the progression of the catheter tip into a branch of the renal artery is called suprase- lective arteriography. The main indication for arteriography is the evaluation of renovascular hypertension (arterial stenoses, arteriovenous fifistulas) or the guidance of

18.2. Imaging methods

18.2.1. Ultrasonography (US, ultra- sound)

Ultrasound is a purely morphological examination that does not provide information about renal function. Far from being a disadvantage, this peculiarity of the method indicates it as a fifirst-line examination whenever necessary to assess renal morphology because it can be applied even to patients with renal failure.

The method’s advantages are fast, cheap, non-radiant and non-invasive and ography.

162 l III. THE EXCRETORY SYSTEM can be applied at the patient’s bed. Ultrasound provides real-time multiplanar morphological information. The Doppler method allows non-invasive exploration of intrarenal flflow. In addition, US allows the guidance of interventional maneuvers.

18. EXAMINATION METHODS AND RADIOLOG

18.2.1.3. Indications

US is the fifirst method of exploration indicated whenever it is necessary to evaluate the urinary tract morphologically and guide most interventional maneuvers.

18.2.2. Nuclear medicine

The techniques of nuclear medicine: scintigraphy, radioisotopic nephrogram, SPECT, PET and fusion imaging, have a well-defifined role in exploring certain diseases of the urinary tract. These techniques are presented in specifific courses in nuclear medicine.

18.2.3. Computed tomography (CT)

Computed tomography is an excellent method of exploring the urinary tract because it provides information about morphology, perfusion and excretion. The disadvantages of the method are that it involves X-rays and iodinated contrast agents. In addition, the costs are higher than IVP or US, and it offers, natively, only cross-sections through the body. Accessibility to the examination may also be more limited than for other examinations.

18.2.3.1. Examination technique

a) The patient’s preparation requires

oral hydration by ingesting 500 - 1000

ml of flfluids 4-12 hours before the

examination. Gases in the digestive

tract are not an impediment. Oral

administration of an iodinated contrast

agent helps outline the digestive tract.

Gastrografifin should be administered

30-60 minutes before the examination. b) The actual examination is carried out

in several stages: i. The native examination (without i.v.

contrast) covers the abdomen and

pelvis, from above the kidneys down

and the amount of injected substance

is visualized 100 sec after injection. v. More than 5 minutes after injection,

the excretory phase is obtained. Late

18.2.3.2. Formation of the CT (and

IVP) image.

The iodinated contrast media (CM) is removed from the blood by glomerular fifiltration. One estimates that in the fifirst hour after injection, 80% of the CM is eliminated. Several factors inflfluence image formation: i. the existence of a suffificiently large num-

ber of functional renal glomeruli,

capable of performing fifiltration; ii. systemic blood pressure (BP = 120 mm

Hg) and glomerular blood pressure

(GBP = 75 mm Hg) - favors glomerular

fifiltration; iii. Colloid osmotic pressure (COP = 25 mm

Hg) - opposes glomerular fifiltration; iv. the hydrostatic pressure of urine in the

urinary tract and the Bowman’s space

(HP = 10 mm Hg) - opposes glo-

merular fifiltration.

The effective fifiltration pressure (EFP) is determined by the relation:

EFP = GBP - (COP + HP)

Normally, EFP = 75 - (25 + 10) = 40 mm Hg.

    18.2.3.3. Functional information provided by CT (and IVP)

    i. The nephrogram defifines the low-intensity opacifification of the renal parenchyma produced by the presence of the blood column containing the contrast medium. Thenephrogramappearsafewsecondsafter the injection of the contrast and persists throughout the exam. The nephrogram of the two kidneys must be symmetrical. The presence of the nephrogram denotes the unhindered penetration of the blood column into the kidneys.

    ii. The pyelogram defifines the highintensity opacifification of the intrarenal urinary tract, from the calyx cups to the origin of the ureter. The pyelogram is well visible and symmetrical on the image obtained at 5 minutes and may persist for 1-2 hours, depending on the urinary flflow. The presence of the pyelogram denotes good glomerular fifiltration and optimal tubular resorption in conditions of normal urinary flflow. Highlighting the intense pyelogram at 5 minutes is improperly referred to as the normal “secretory function.”

    The pyelogram is poorly defifined or even invisible in hyperhydration or severe defificit of tubular resorption function (isoor hyposthenuria).

    iii. The evacuation function defifines the elimination of the CM from the kidneys to the bladder. Normal evacuation function means the presence, on the 5 minutes scan, of the contrast substance in both ureters and the bladder. The ureters are fragmentarily opaque and the bladder is incompletely fifilled.

    18.2.3.4. Anatomy

    i. Natively, the kidneys appear as oval masses with a density of soft tissues in the paravertebral spaces. The renal contour is smooth. In each kidney, the renal sinus appears hypodense and continues, in the middle part of the kidney, through the renal hilum, with the renal vessels. There is no difference in density between the cortex and the renal medulla.

    ii. In the corticomedullary phase, there is a noticeable difference in density between cortex (iodophilic) and medulla (less iodophilic). This phase is used to obtain CT angiography.

    18.2.4. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

    The method allows multiplanar morphological exploration of the kidneys and urinary tract and obtaining images of the urinary tract similar to those of the Uro CT, with or without the use of the contrast agent (UroMR). The use of paramagnetic contrast agents allows the performance of MRI angiography. 19.1. Opacity changes

19.1.1.Additional opacities (focal)

19.1.1.1. Calcifific opacities are visible on KUB. For their detection, examination without CM administration is mandatory, both in conventional radiology and CT.

a) Urinary stones. Kidney stones can be radiopaque or radiolucent. Only radiopaque stones are detected on examinations without CM. They are composed of Ca oxalate, Ca phosphate, ammoniac-magnesian phospha168 l III. THE EXCRETORY SYSTEM tes or mixed. Radiolucent stones are made up of cystine, uric acid or cholesterol. The IVP may suggest their presence, but the preferred methods for their detection are US or CT. By defifinition, stones are located in the lumen of the urinary tract: calyx, pelvis, ureter or bladder. The dimensions of the stones vary from very small, millimetric (calyx) to a few centimeters (pelvic stones). Very large stones, usually made up of multiple fragments, which mold the excretory cavities, are called staghorn stones. The shape and contour of the stones are varied: spherical, oval or polygonal.

Examination techniques used:

i. KUB is the cheapest and fastest method for detecting and locating radiopaque stones (fifigure 136).

ii. IVP can detect the presence of radiolucent stones as urinary tract fifilling

The method is benefificial to defifine the consequences of the presence of stones on the urinary tract: obstruction in the discharge, associated with urinary stasis and upstream segmental dilation hydronephrosis. Impairment of ipsilateral renal function is also frequently observed, especially in patients with renal colic (fifigure 137).

iii. US is used in emergencies, often as a fifirst-line method, in urinary colic. It can detect the presence of stones, regardless of their chemical composition. Diffificulties may occur only in the case of stones migrated into the ureters. a) The cavern is characteristic of tuberculosis;

Imaging In Kidney Transplantation

Andrei Lebovici

20.1 Imaging in living-related kidney donor

Initially, an ultrasound is performed for parenchyma analysis followed by CT angiography to visualize arterial and venous anatomy.

In a kidney with a single simple cortical cyst or moderate reflflux nephropathy with a single scar, the affected kidney will be the one chosen for transplant.

In the case of a duplex collecting system, the contralateral kidney will be transplanted. Approximately 20% of the kidneys have accessory renal arteries; the kidney with a single artery is easier to transplant.

20.2. Surgical technique

The transplanted kidney is located in the iliac fossa, usually, the right kidney is placed in the left iliac fossa and vice versa. This way, vascular anastomoses are easier to perform.

The renal pelvis is located anteriorly for the transplanted kidney, the renal artery posterior to the pelvis and the renal vein the most posterior element of the renal sinus, resulting in an inverse position compared to normal.

The renal artery is anastomosed end to side onto the common or external iliac artery.

The renal vein is anastomosed end to side onto the external iliac vein.

The ureter can be implanted directly into the bladder or using a submucosal tunnel (Politano-Ledbetter technique) to reduce reflflux.

20.3. Imaging of the dysfunctional transplanted kidney

Kidney transplant dysfunction can present with a rising serum creatinine level, decreasing urine output, pain and tenderness over the graft.

Imaging modalities to work up graft dysfunction include ultrasonography, computed tomography, nuclear medicine or molecular imaging, angiography and magnetic resonance imaging.

Due to the superfificial position of the transplanted kidney, ultrasonography represents the imaging method of choice in analyzing the transplanted kidney and its complications.
